interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: SciForge: An AI-Native, Multimodal Workbench for Scientific Discovery
papers.authors: SciForge Team : Zhangyang Gao , Minghao Fang , Yifei Liu , Hanhui Yang , Xinyu Gu , Shixiang Tang , Siqi Sun , Lei Bai , Cheng Tan , Mengdi Liu , Hao Wu , Shuizhou Chen
papers.abstract: Scientific work increasingly spans heterogeneous artifacts -- papers, code, datasets, scientific file formats, model outputs, figures, manuscripts, and team decisions -- yet general-purpose AI assistants rarely preserve these objects as a coherent, auditable research state. We present SciForge, a multimodal research-native AI workbench that reserves the graphical interface for human judgment while search, parsing, model routing, workflow execution, plotting, writing, and presentation generation run as modular agent-accessible services. SciForge is built around five pillars: (i) \emph{goal-scoped scientific decision governance} for \textbf{goal-oriented} research, with review gates and shared review surfaces; (ii) \emph{translate-then-reason} for \textbf{multimodal} input, routing scientific objects through domain translators before the agent reasons; (iii) \emph{evidence governance} for \textbf{auditable} traceability, linking claims to provenance chains and audit findings; (iv) \emph{collaborative team science} for \textbf{collaborative} research, enabling multi-role decision governance, with shared team workspaces planned for future releases; and (v) \emph{real-world application scenarios} for \textbf{practical} impact, demonstrated through eight end-to-end user cases, with flagship demonstrations including multi-day agentic research sprints for gene discovery, AI-guided de novo protein design, molecular optimization, and genome-to-BGC discovery. The system combines a thin interaction layer, contextual research capability patterns, an Agent Runtime and Workflow Engine, an Evidence-DAG audit sidecar and a Scientific Model Router. SciForge currently runs as a desktop application, with mobile supervision support; future releases will deepen team collaboration. The system is open-source and available at this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: This paper directly addresses AI-native scientific workbenches with multimodal capabilities, agentic workflows, and auditable research state, which aligns perfectly with my interest in LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, and reproducible research in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks how to build a research-native AI workbench that preserves all scientific artifacts (papers, code, datasets, figures, model outputs) as a coherent, auditable state. The main idea is SciForge, a system with modular agent-accessible services for search, parsing, model routing, workflow execution, plotting, writing, and presentation, governed by goal-scoped decision gates and evidence-DAG audit trails. For astronomy, this could revolutionize how we combine JWST imaging, spectra, catalogs, and literature in a single reproducible workflow. One could imagine using SciForge to design a multi-day agentic research sprint for identifying and characterizing high-redshift AGN in JWST data, with automatic provenance tracking. However, the system is currently a desktop application and may require significant adaptation for astronomical data formats and large survey datasets.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the Evidence-DAG audit sidecar and how it links claims to provenance chains, which is critical for reproducible astronomy.
Check the Scientific Model Router and whether it can interface with astronomical analysis tools (e.g., CIGALE, EAZY, Prospector).
Examine the eight end-to-end user cases to see if any involve image or spectral data similar to astronomy.
Assess the system's ability to handle large astronomical catalogs (e.g., millions of sources) and multimodal data (images + spectra + tables).

papers.title: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
papers.authors: Hyunin Lee , Jinglue Xu , Jeffrey Seely , Donghyun Lee , Matei Zaharia , Yujin Tang
papers.abstract: Under model--harness co-evolution, harnesses are not merely inference-time scaffolds but data-generating components whose execution traces can shape future foundation models. This motivates harness-in-the-loop learning: optimizing harnesses for both immediate agent performance and the quality of traces used for future model training. However, continually updating provider-built scaffolds is costly and labor-intensive. We therefore investigate whether optimizing user-constructed harnesses in a task-specific manner can improve execution-trace quality while remaining computationally lightweight and requiring only a few update iterations. To this end, we introduce Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI), which represents the harness as a prompt-level specification of the agent loop and iteratively refines it using pairwise feedback over its own revision history. Across 30 synthetic machine-learning research tasks spanning quantitative finance, robotics, and pharmacy, a few RHI iterations suffice to substantially raise the performance ceiling of low-reasoning-effort agents, exceeding the corresponding maximum-reasoning-effort setting while reducing inference cost by up to 60%. We show that these gains arise primarily from improved task-specific context management through more effective inter-agent information flow rather than longer reasoning traces. Finally, we formalize this behavior as an information-theoretic hypothesis for RHI's implicit optimization objective, suggesting RHI as a practical algorithm for continual learning within the paradigm of model--harness co-evolution.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to building LLM agents for scientific research. The idea of recursively improving the 'harness' (prompt-level specification of the agent loop) could be applied to astronomical data analysis or literature review agents.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI), a method to iteratively refine the prompt-level specification of an LLM agent loop using pairwise feedback. It shows that a few iterations can substantially improve agent performance on synthetic ML research tasks, reducing inference cost. For astronomy, this could be used to automatically improve the prompts and workflows of agents that analyze JWST data or search the literature. A caveat is that the method is demonstrated on synthetic tasks; its effectiveness on real astronomical workflows (with messy data and domain-specific constraints) needs validation.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method is tested on real-world scientific tasks or only synthetic ones.
Look for the specific feedback mechanism (pairwise comparisons) and whether it requires human annotation or can be automated.
Assess the computational cost of the iterative refinement process.

papers.title: Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models
papers.authors: Wes Gurnee , Nicholas Sofroniew , Adam Pearce , Mateusz Piotrowski , Isaac Kauvar , Runjin Chen , Anna Soligo , Paul Bogdan , Euan Ong , Rowan Wang , Ben Thompson , David Abrahams , Subhash Kantamneni , Emmanuel Ameisen , Joshua Batson , Jack Lindsey
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: Out of everything the human brain processes, only a small fraction is consciously accessible, in the sense of being available for verbal report, deliberate control, and flexible reasoning. In this paper, we present evidence that an analogous functional distinction has emerged in large language models. Using a new interpretability technique, the Jacobian lens, we identify the representations a model is poised to verbalize at any point in its processing. These representations, which we collectively call the J-space, exhibit the functional properties characteristic of a global workspace: their contents can be reported, deliberately summoned and held, used to carry the intermediate steps of silent reasoning, and passed as arguments to arbitrary downstream computations, while automatic processing such as text parsing and routine inference proceeds without them. The J-space also has structural signatures that global workspace theory associates with conscious access: it carries coherent content only in an intermediate band of layers, holds on the order of tens of concepts at a time, and is broadcast by the model's weights more widely than other representations. These properties make it a practical window into a model's unspoken thinking. In alignment audits, it reveals strategic deliberation, evaluation awareness, and trained-in misaligned dispositions that never appear in the model's outputs. We find that post-training installs the Assistant's point of view in the workspace, and we introduce counterfactual reflection training, which improves behavior by training only what a model would say if interrupted and asked to reflect. These results indicate that language models maintain a small, privileged set of representations bearing some of the functional hallmarks of conscious access, and that decoding these representations sheds light on ongoing cognitive processes.
papers.Reasons for match: Relevant for understanding internal representations in LLMs, which could inform how LLM agents for astronomy reason and whether they can be trusted. The concept of a 'global workspace' could help design more interpretable scientific agents.
papers.Short digest: This paper identifies a set of representations in LLMs (called J-space) that function like a global workspace: they are available for verbal report, deliberate control, and reasoning, while automatic processing happens separately. The authors show these representations can reveal hidden reasoning, including misaligned intentions. For astronomy, this could help build more transparent LLM agents for data analysis, by providing a window into the model's 'unspoken thinking'. However, the method requires access to model internals (activations), which may not be available for all models.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the Jacobian lens technique is model-agnostic or requires specific architecture access.
Look for demonstrations of detecting 'strategic deliberation' or 'evaluation awareness' in a scientific context (e.g., reasoning about data).

papers.title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification
papers.authors: Nicolas Boullé , Diana Halikias , Samuel E. Otto , Alex Townsend
papers.subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Dynamical Systems (math.DS)
papers.abstract: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate for any recovered model. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.
papers.Reasons for match: Theoretical paper on system identification from one experiment; zero-one law could inform whether a single astronomical observation can uniquely determine model parameters, relevant for parameter estimation and model selection.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses whether a model can be identified from a single input-response experiment, focusing on analytic systems linearly parameterized by dictionary terms. The authors prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This provides an a posteriori certificate for any recovered model. For astronomy, this theory could be applied to determine whether a single observation (e.g., a spectrum or light curve) can uniquely constrain a model of a galaxy or AGN. A concrete workflow might involve using the zero-one law to check if a given observational setup can uniquely determine parameters of a high-redshift galaxy model. However, the paper is theoretical and may require significant effort to apply to specific astronomical problems.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the zero-one law applies to the types of models used in astronomy (e.g., SED fitting, dynamical models).
Look for details on the dictionary terms and whether they can represent astronomical models.
Examine the numerical examples to see if they include any astronomical or geophysical cases.

papers.title: Diffusion models recover accurate mixture weights despite score function insensitivity
papers.authors: Andrew Dennehy , Ramchandran Muthukumar , Rebecca Willett , Nisha Chandramoorthy
papers.abstract: Score-based generative models exhibit a puzzling behavior: they often appear to cover all modes of a target multimodal distribution and yet may fail to learn the correct relative mode amplitudes, which can be interpreted as mixture weights. We resolve this apparent paradox by relating the diffusion score matching (DSM) loss to the error in estimating mixture weights from generated samples. We show that, even when the target score is insensitive to mixture weights, generated samples can recover the weights accurately if the scores at intermediate noise levels are informative about the weights. Accordingly, we define the diffusion score sensitivity index (DSSI) as the variation in the DSM loss relative to changes in a parameter. We then show that the DSSI governs the accuracy with which the parameter of the target distribution can be estimated from generated samples. For Gaussian mixtures in arbitrary dimensions, we prove that the mixture weight estimation errors are on the same order as the DSM loss under mild conditions. Empirically, we show the emergence of sensitivity during the noising process of benchmark data distributions under typical noise schedules, and that these sensitivity values predict how well a well-trained model recovers mixture weights. Furthermore, we show that the choice of noise schedule can reduce diffusion sensitivity, leading to mode amplification. Although we focus on mixture weights, the proposed sensitivity framework governs the recovery of any qualitative parameter of the target distribution.
papers.Reasons for match: Relevant to understanding generative models (diffusion models) which are used for astronomical image generation and anomaly detection. The focus on mixture weights could relate to population-level inference in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper explains why diffusion models can recover correct mixture weights (e.g., relative proportions of different galaxy types) even when the score function appears insensitive to them. It introduces a sensitivity index (DSSI) that governs how well a parameter can be estimated from generated samples. For astronomy, this is important because diffusion models are used to generate synthetic galaxy images or spectra, and we need to trust that the relative frequencies of rare vs. common objects are accurate. A caveat is that the theory is proven for Gaussian mixtures; real astronomical data may have more complex distributions.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for empirical validation on non-Gaussian or real-world datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, ImageNet) to gauge generality.
Check whether the noise schedule analysis provides practical guidance for training astronomical diffusion models.
